progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: C10 (Ka = [H₃O⁺][A⁻] / [HA] for a weak acid; pKa = −log Ka; ethanoic acid Ka 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ and pKa 4.74; the decimal-places rule applied to Ka). C08 (a weak acid stays mostly un-ionised; the particle lens). C07 (pH from [H₃O⁺]; the decimal-places rule; 1.0 mol/L HCl gives [H₃O⁺] = c). C06 (conjugate pairs; the conjugate base of a weak acid pulls protons back, the conjugate base of a strong acid has almost no pull). C05 (strong and weak; salts dissolve completely into ions). C02 (salt names: sodium ethanoate, ammonium chloride). Module 5: Le Chatelier's principle (adding a product shifts an equilibrium back). Year 11: n = c × V. Not assumed: the word buffer, capacity, the blood buffer. Also from C08: the ICE table, which is why scene 5 says the amounts put in can be used directly (the partners barely react with water).
progression.startsWith: Add acid or base to a weak-acid/conjugate-base mixture. The video opens: Two beakers, a hundred millilitres each. One is pure water, at pH seven. The other is a mix of ethanoic acid and sodium ethanoate, at pH four point seven four.
progression.stopsAfter: describing a buffer as a weak acid and its conjugate base in large amounts; writing the equations for added acid (taken up by the conjugate base) and added base (taken up by the weak acid); explaining why the pH changes only slightly, using [H₃O⁺] = Ka × n(HA) / n(A⁻); estimating a buffer's pH (pH = pKa for equal amounts; below or above pKa otherwise) and calculating the pH after a small addition; explaining why a strong acid with its salt is not a buffer; explaining capacity and why it depends on the amounts, not the pH; describing how the carbonic acid and hydrogencarbonate buffer keeps blood pH 7.35 to 7.45, with the lungs and kidneys topping it up, and naming buffering in cells and oceans; reading buffer-against-water evidence. No bench preparation or risk table (chem-m6-p05), no Henderson-Hasselbalch log form, no partial neutralisation or half-equivalence (chem-m6-c14), no polyprotic calculations.
progression.nextLesson: preparing a buffer in the lab and testing it against water (route chem-m6-p05).

teaching.task: The same splash of acid drops water by five pH units, but a mixture of ethanoic acid and sodium ethanoate by less than a tenth. What does that mixture contain, how does it take up added acid and base, what sets its pH, when does it run out, and why does your blood depend on one?
teaching.causalExplanation: (1) the same acid drops water 5 pH units and the mixture less than 0.1: why? (1); (2) ethanoic acid stays mostly whole and the salt supplies plenty of ethanoate, so both partners are present in large amounts: a buffer (2); (3) added hydronium meets ethanoate, the conjugate base of a weak acid, which takes the proton back; almost all of it is used up (3); (4) added hydroxide takes a proton from ethanoic acid; a defender for each attack; water against buffer for base too (4); (5) Ka rearranged: [H₃O⁺] = Ka × acid ÷ base; moles work because the volume cancels; equal amounts give pH = pKa (5); (6) after the acid the ratio is about 1.2, so hydronium rises by about 20%, against a hundred thousand times in water (6); (7) the ratio sets the pH, so buffers need not be neutral; a strong acid's conjugate base does not take protons back, so HCl with NaCl is not a buffer (7); (8) each portion of acid uses up ethanoate; when it runs out, the pH plunges: capacity depends on the amounts (8); (9) blood keeps pH 7.35 to 7.45 with carbonic acid and hydrogencarbonate; the CO₂ formed is breathed out (9); (10) blood has about 20 hydrogencarbonate ions for each dissolved carbon dioxide molecule (carbon dioxide and carbonic acid together are the acid side), so it absorbs acid better than base; it is topped up by lungs and kidneys; cells and oceans buffer too (10); memory aid (11); two attempts and brief feedback (12 to 15); decision rule and handoff (16); key notes (17).
teaching.conversationalApproach: one contrast carries the video: the same millilitre of hydrochloric acid drops water by five pH units but a mixture of ethanoic acid and sodium ethanoate by less than a tenth. The particle lens shows why (ethanoate, the conjugate base of a weak acid, takes back the added hydronium; ethanoic acid gives a proton to added hydroxide: a defender for each attack), the Ka expression rearranged shows that the pH follows the ratio of acid to base, and a worked example finds the pH after the acid. Repeated portions of acid then use up the ethanoate until the pH plunges (capacity), and the blood buffer applies the same reasoning with the lungs and kidneys topping it up. Two exam questions follow with brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: Two beakers, a hundred millilitres each. One is pure water, at pH seven. The other is a mix of ethanoic acid and sodium ethanoate, at pH four point seven four. Add one millilitre of one mole per litre hydrochloric acid to each. The water drops to pH two point zero zero, five whole units. The mixture drops to four point six six, less than a tenth of a unit. So what's in that second beaker that soaks up the acid, and can it ever run out?
teaching.understandingCheck: (A1) "A solution contains 0.20 mol/L ammonia (NH₃) and 0.20 mol/L ammonium chloride (NH₄Cl). (a) Explain, using equations, how this solution resists a change in pH when a small amount of hydrochloric acid or sodium hydroxide is added. (b) Estimate the pH of the solution, given that the pKa of NH₄⁺ is 9.25 at 25 °C." New pair (a basic buffer, weak base and conjugate acid; not shown anywhere before the attempt), so the student must find which partner is the acid. Crossed mistake: "NH₄⁺ + H₃O⁺ → ..." (partners swapped; the site's "HA reacts with added H⁺" misconception). (A2) "Two buffer solutions, X and Y, each have a volume of 100 mL and a pH of 4.74 at 25 °C. X contains 0.010 mol of ethanoic acid and 0.010 mol of sodium ethanoate. Y contains 0.0010 mol of ethanoic acid and 0.0010 mol of sodium ethanoate. A student adds 0.0020 mol of hydrochloric acid to each solution. Predict and explain the change in pH in each solution. Assume the volume does not change. Ka(CH₃COOH) = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵." Tests capacity against pH. Crossed mistake: "same pH, so they resist equally".
teaching.curriculumScope: Syllabus (NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017), as printed: "conduct a practical investigation to prepare a buffer and demonstrate its properties (ACSCH080)" "describe the importance of buffers in natural systems (ACSCH098, ACSCH102)" this video starts from the route's acid or base added to a weak acid and conjugate base mixture and stops at explaining the response, estimating the pH and identifying the capacity limit. It teaches: what a buffer contains and why (a weak acid mostly whole, plus its conjugate base from a dissolved salt; C05 and C06 callbacks); how the conjugate base takes up added hydronium and the weak acid takes up added hydroxide, with equations (the Le Chatelier reading is a Module 5 callback, one clause); why the pH still changes a little (the Ka expression rearranged, [H₃O⁺] = Ka × n(HA) / n(A⁻), a C10 callback, with moles in place of concentrations because the volume cancels); pH = pKa when the partners are equal, and the direction of the pH when they are not; why a strong acid with its salt is not a buffer (C06 conjugate strength); buffer capacity and its limit, shown as the pH curve for repeated acid portions against water; why capacity depends on the amounts, not the pH; the blood buffer (carbonic acid and hydrogencarbonate, the lungs and kidneys) and the importance of buffers in natural systems; the demonstration evidence the practical dotpoint asks for (the same addition to buffer and to water, side by side). Not here: preparing a buffer at the bench, the risk table and the dilution test (chem-m6-p05, the next video, which owns the practical conduct; this video shows the comparison data only); the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation by name or in log form (site card 3 labels it Extension; see Open decisions); partial neutralisation to make a buffer and half-equivalence (chem-m6-c14, titration curves); quantitative buffer range "pKa ± 1"; polyprotic acids and the phosphate calculation of site worked example 2; the direction of an amphiprotic ion from Ka against Kb (C10 deferred it here; see Open decisions); detailed blood-gas clinical cases (site worked example 3, diabetic ketoacidosis) and ocean saturation chemistry (worksheet 04 corrections).

design.visualSystem: Explainer engine: warm paper stage, handwritten Caveat headings, amber doodle layer. Colour key on screen throughout: H₃O⁺ teal token on pale blue water (C01); OH⁻ violet; whole ethanoic acid molecules amber-outlined (C05, C08); ethanoate grey-violet; Na⁺ and Cl⁻ small grey spectators; meter readouts amber digits; the ratio bar's acid column amber and base column grey-violet; water's lines and readouts pale blue, the buffer's teal. Board layout (constant, C03, C07, C08 and C10): top-left the short task line; the left column holds the givens card during worked examples (grouped, units attached); the centre holds the lens, the ratio bar, the graph or the working, one stage per line, earlier lines dimming; a plate sits small at the right only when it carries the explanation. Clutter rule: at most three text items bright at once; every label fades when its sentence ends. Reuse: painted plates (inspected 20 Oct): `m6-ph-meter-probe-beaker-v1.png` (two copies: hook and scene 4, coded amber readouts "7.00" → "2.00" or "12.00" on the water and "4.74" → "4.66" or "4.83" on the buffer; beakers labelled in code "water, 100 mL" and "ethanoic acid + sodium ethanoate, 0.100 mol/L each, 100 mL"), `m6-beaker-v1.png` (scene 2, under the lens), `m6-vinegar-bottle-v1.png` (not used), `m5x-ammonia-bottle-v1.png` (attempt 1 card, small), `m5x-red-blood-cells-v1.png` (inspected: five painted red blood cells, no person; scene 9, small), `m8-lungs-healthy-v1.png` (inspected: a painted pair of lungs with trachea and bronchi, no person or face; scenes 9 and 10, small, the CO₂ arrow ends at it). No new plates needed. No human figures.
